fields.expected: Use 'farther'. 'A lot' strengthens the comparison of the new and old distances to school.
Use 'the most slowly'. 'Of all the beginners' compares Chloe with the whole group, so use a superlative adverb to describe how she would learn.
Use 'the most popular'. It shows that Golden Wok's food was more popular than the food from both other companies.
Use 'the most reliably'. This superlative adverb shows that Golden Wok's delivery was more reliable than either of the other companies' delivery.
Use 'had' for possession at the earlier train journey. Tapping the card shows that Kelvin had it then.
Use 'am searching' for the search in progress now. With 'I', the present continuous is am + the -ing form.
Use 'keep' to state the MTR staff's usual practice in the present simple.
Use 'is ringing' for the sound happening now. The singular noun 'bell' takes is + the -ing form.
Use 'Did you use' to ask about an earlier action at recess. Use did + the base verb use.
Use 'didn't buy' for the earlier action. Didn't means did not and is followed by the base verb buy.
Use 'packs' to describe Mum's regular habit. With 'my mum', add -s to the verb in the present simple.
Use 'didn't notice' for the earlier train journey. Didn't means did not and is followed by the base verb notice.
Use 'is watching'. Now shows that Dad's action is happening at this moment.
Use 'is drawing'. Kitty's sister is drawing at the moment, so use the present continuous.
Use 'didn't believe'. This describes Kitty's reaction in the past; after didn't, use the base verb believe.
Use 'stay'. The present simple describes the family's usual habit during typhoons; 'family' can take plural agreement in British English.
Use 'isn't'. Dad is giving a general safety rule; use is with the singular subject it.
Use 'didn't reply'. The reply was delayed, so use didn't + the base verb reply.
Use 'fell' to describe the result of the incident. Fell is the past simple form of fall.
Use 'gave' to describe the completed action. Gave is the past simple form of give.
Use 'doesn't like'. Grandma is one person, so use doesn't + the base verb like.
Use 'am sitting'. 'Right now' shows that the action is happening at this moment.
Use 'have' for the family's Sunday habit. With 'we', the simple present uses the base form have.
Use 'is pouring'. 'At the moment' shows an action happening now, and Grandpa takes is.
Use 'bumped' to describe the completed bump. Bumped is the past simple form of bump.
Use 'comes'. 'Usually' describes a regular result, and 'comes' treats Blue House as one team.
Use 'to enter'. 'Plan to + verb' describes what the team intends to do.
Use 'Paddling'. The -ing phrase 'Paddling for two hours in the summer heat' is the subject of 'is really tiring'.
Use 'to hold'. 'Managed to + verb' means Carmen succeeded in doing something.
Use 'Spending'. The verb-ing phrase 'Spending time with the elderly' is the subject and names the activity that turned out to be fun.
Use 'to revise'. 'Plan to + verb' describes what you intend to do.
Use 'to take'. 'Threaten to + verb' describes an action someone says they may take.
Use 'Working'. The -ing phrase names the activity and is the subject of 'helps'.
Use 'to be'. 'Too forgetful to be in charge' means Jacky is not reliable enough to manage the list.
Use 'to order'. Owen uses 'want to + verb' to say what he would like to do.
Use 'collecting'. 'Collecting 32 cards in one week' is the subject of 'won't be easy'.
Use 'saying'. The -ing form names the activity the class can practise.
Use 'did not want'. His reluctance ended last September, so use the simple past for this finished period.
Use 'has not missed'. 'So far' means up to now, so use the present perfect for his attendance.
Use 'has not decided'. 'Yet' shows that her decision is still unresolved at the time of speaking.
Use 'has run'. 'Since 1998' links Mr Chan's management of the café from that year up to the present.
Use 'have not replied'. 'Yet' shows that the reply is still outstanding now, so use have not + the past participle replied.
Use 'has lived'. 'Since she was born' links Granny Leung's residence from birth up to now, so use has + the past participle lived.
Use 'have not bought'. 'Since the beginning of this year' describes the period up to now, so use the present perfect.
Use 'did not give'. The wait ended when Mum agreed in February, so use the simple past for that completed period.
